stem: When you wave a sparkler quickly in the dark, you briefly see a continuous trail of light rather than separate points — because the visual impression persists for a fraction of a second after the stimulus is gone. This very brief, high-capacity initial memory store is called:
explanation: Sensory memory holds an almost exact copy of sensory input for a very brief moment (iconic memory for vision, echoic memory for hearing) before it decays or is passed to short-term memory via attention — the first of the three memory stages.

section: Educational Psychology · Ch10 — Three-Stage Memory Model (Complete)
subject: Educational Psychology
stem: According to the classic Atkinson-Shiffrin multi-store model of memory, information flows through which sequence of stores?

options.option_text: Sensory memory → Short-term memory → Long-term memory
Long-term memory → Short-term memory → Sensory memory
Short-term memory → Sensory memory → Long-term memory
There is only one single memory store with no distinct stages

explanation: The Atkinson-Shiffrin model proposes information first enters sensory memory (very brief), then, with attention, passes to short-term/working memory (limited capacity, brief), and finally, with rehearsal/encoding, to long-term memory (large capacity, durable).

stem: A student who was momentarily distracted can still 'replay' the last few words a teacher just said, even though attention had briefly wandered. This brief auditory sensory store is specifically called:
explanation: Echoic memory is the auditory form of sensory memory, briefly retaining sound information (slightly longer than iconic/visual sensory memory) — allowing a person to 'replay' recently heard sounds even after a momentary lapse in attention.
